sections.text: Subduing their senses, viewing all conditions of life with the same eye, and working for the welfare of all beings, assuredly they come to Me.
But they who thus fix their attention on the Absolute and Impersonal encounter greater hardships, for it is difficult for those who possess a body to realise Me as without one.
ये तु सर्वाणि कर्माणि मयि संन्यस्य मत्परः।
Verily, those who surrender their actions to Me, who muse on Me, worship Me and meditate on Me alone, with no thought save of Me,

What is my purpose and destiny? So we had been discussing chapter one, Arjunas Grief -- Arjuna Vishada yoga. This is a contradictory term: Vishada and Yoga. Grief cannot be in Yoga; we are always in Yoga.
But when we are in grief, this is the one time we really align ourselves to our own self, seeking an answer: how do I get out of this grief? So grief also is one form of yoga. In fact, it aligns you more to your own reality than when times are good, when we are more outwardly seeking things outside. When we are in grief, we seek inward and ask, how do I get out of this sorrow and find peace? So therefore this chapter is also called Yoga -- the Yoga of Arjunas Grief.
And the grief basically started with his looking at his situation. So far we have seen that Dhritarashtra was curious about whats going on, out of his ignorance about whats happening. Curiosity is the manifestation of ignorance.
Unless we are ignorant, we cannot be curious. We can only be curious about something we are ignorant about. We cannot be curious about something we already know.
So Dhritarashtra, being ignorant about whats going on, hes curious about whats happening at the battlefield of Kurukshetra, he asked Sanjaya. And then what we have seen is Sanjays narration. Sanjaya first narrated what Duryodhan was doing.
Duryodhana has gauged his situation, came to the conclusion we may not have enough resources. And then Bheeshma declared the war by blowing his own conch. And once he blew his conch, everybody blew their own conch.
Now we have seen that the situation is such that everybody blew their own conches. And there was so much sound, there was so much chaos that everybody was trembling with fear. Now we are coming back to what Arjuna is doing.
The last three verses say Vyavasthitan, Dhrushtva, Dhartarashtra, and Kapidhvajah. Having seen this -- the army of Duryodhana, Dhritarashtras side, the Kaurava army assembled in the battlefield -- Kapidhvajah, the one whose flag has a monkey, Hanuman. Basically, Hanuman is a symbol of air, Marutasya putrah.
So basically his symbol says: my chariot flies like wind -- that powerful chariot, thats his symbol. So the one whose symbol is Kapidhvajah, Arjuna -- pravritte shastra sampate dhanuh udyamya pandavah. He saw that the people are ready to discharge their weapons, war is declared, everybody is anxious.
And as I said, always the first person has to do something. One person blows the conch, everybody blows conches. The first person shoots an arrow, everybody starts shooting.
Nobody has shot the arrow yet, but everybody is anxious to discharge their weapons. So Arjuna also picks up his Gandiva. And then he says, Hrishikesham tada vakyam idam aha Mahipate -- O King.
Sanjaya is addressing Dhritarashtra. Now that Arjuna has seen this army assembled in front of him, ready to discharge weapons, he has picked up his Gandiva. Basically, hes ready.
He probably wants to be the first one to shoot an arrow -- picks up the Gandiva. But then, as any good commander, he wants to make sure he has a complete understanding of whats going on. So then he says -- he said the following sentence to Hrishikesha Krishna, the one with the short hair.
Now this is a half verse. This is where Sanjaya stops. Then we go straight to Arjuna.
So sometimes we hear Sanjayas commentary; sometimes Sanjaya just puts it directly so we can listen to what Arjuna is saying or Krishna is saying. Arjuna uvacha: Senayoh ubhayoh madhye ratham sthapaya me Achyuta -- O Achyuta, another name of Krishna meaning one who never fails you -- take my chariot and station it right in the middle of the two armies. This is basically something any general would do.
When we are ready to attack Iraq or Iran, we say, Oh, we know they have WMDs. Well, we have the satellites to figure it out. We concluded that Saddam Hussein has all those WMDs -- weapons of mass destruction. And now therefore we are ready to attack him.
Similarly, Arjuna said, well, let me be in a position where I can gauge the complete situation of who I have to fight so that I can strategize accordingly. Anxious soldier, anxious warrior, very confident, ready to discharge his arrow. He just wants his chariot to be in a proper location.
And he shows his confidence. He says may ratham my ratha. So he is a commander who is ready to give his command and do his duty.
Yavat etan niriksheham. Why I wanted to do that because I would like to see Yudhung kaman, avasthitaan, which generals, which warriors are assembled in the other army. Obviously they didnt have satellite pictures.
You have to have eye contact to figure out whats happening. So you need a station point where your perspective is panoramic, where you can see everybody. So therefore its a put me in a position where I can panoramically see who are assembled here.
Duryodhana has already done that. Duryodhana went through who are on the other side. We havent heard from Arjuna.
Now Arjuna says I want to say Kair maya saha yuddhavyam asmin ranam samuddya me who are desirous of fighting at the eve of this battle. Eve of the battle, at just the beginning of this battle. Let me know with whom I must fight, who Im going to fight.
Yotsyamanam aveksheham ye ete atra samagatah Dhartarashtrasya durbuddher yuddhe priyachikirshavah. He shows his disgust for the people who are in their wrong notion. Yotsyamanam avekshe aham -- because I would like to observe those who are assembled.
Ye ete atra samagatah -- theyre assembled here. Dhartarashtrasya durbuddheh priya chikirshavah -- who are here to fight, wishing to please in battle the evil-minded son of Dhritarashtra. They are pleasing somebody who has an evil mind -- Duryodhana.
They are not really using their own judgment about what is right and wrong. They just want to please somebody, whether he is wrong or right, just because he is in power, just because he is someone they need to align with. So I want to see who those people are.
Verse 24 onward is Sanjaya Vachana. We are getting back to Sanjaya: Evam uktva Hrishikesham Gudakesha Bharata senayoh ubhayoh madhye sthapayitva rathottamam. Just as he said, Krishna established the chariot thus addressed by Gurakesha.
Just as instructed by Arjuna. Shikesha situated the best of the chariots between the two armies. This is where the turning point is.
Here is how he sees what the situation is. Sometimes in our ignorance we are very comfortable in what we are doing because we do not know the rest of the story. So we are very gung-ho on doing something.
It is suddenly when we have the complete picture that what Im doing is not just truly good -- it can also affect people. Go ahead and have this gas pipeline or whatever. The fracked gas looks very good.
But its when you have the complete picture of how many people get affected by it, what the effect on the natural resources is -- Then you start questioning whether that is the right thing to do or the wrong thing to do. Till Arjuna did not have the clear picture, he was very gung-ho: I want to fight this battle. Ill kill those people who are aligning with this Durbuddhi. We will see what happens.
We completed chapter 11, Vishwarupa Darshan. Now we have started discussing chapter 12, Bhakti Yoga. So we have learned so far in Bhagavad Gita about our limited self -- in the first portion, up to chapter five.
Then it culminated into Dhyana Yoga. Once you know about the makeup of your being, you have to contemplate upon who I am. Everything we learned in that portion says that what I have considered myself to be so far is not me.
Everything I considered as me -- this body, this mind, this intellect, my accomplishments, my relationships -- all this I considered to be me. And it turned out it is not me. I is something other than all these things.
So contemplate upon the idea about who I am, that I am something other than this body, other than this mind, other than this intellect. And in that contemplation, what I find is myself. When I negate all the things which I currently consider as me, but turned out to be my equipment, my achievement, my accomplishment, my relationship, you negate all of that.
And then what is left is Me. And that I is no different than the Supreme I. Thats what we learned in that segment of Bhagavad Gita.
So the next segment, which we embarked on learning was to know about the nature of the Supreme Self and how I can relate myself to the Supreme Self. So we have learned that his nature is imperishable, immutable, all pervading, omnipresent, omniscient. And everything in my world that I know is strung into him like the beads and necklace.
So that segment, after discussing the nature of the self, ended with chapter 11 which showed the totality of that vision. If I have that identification not with the limited self but with the greater self, what will be my vision of that Supreme Purusha, the Ultimate Being? Everything will be included in it. Once I have that understanding of the relationship between my limited self and that supreme self, it has to culminate in devotion toward the Supreme Self.
Once I identify with the supreme self, Ill be devoted to that supreme self. So the next chapter is Bhakti Yoga, the Yoga of devotion. But most of us really get scared by the very word bhakti.
Because unlike Gnana and Karma, where I have some control, I have control over actions. At least I know that when I want to act, I will have the ability to act. It will be my will to engage in actions, so I can motivate myself to act.
There is something I can do about it. Same way with knowledge -- I think I have some control; I can learn when I want to know. If I think Im ignorant about something and I really want to become knowledgeable, there are means available to me.
If I can engage in it, then obviously I will get the knowledge. So with Gnana and Karma, we feel somewhat comfortable because we have something to say about it, some way to engage. But when it comes to bhakti, we are completely lost.
Bhakti is an emotional response, and emotions are not something I have control over. Thats what I learned all my life that why did you do that, Rajan? Because I couldnt control my emotions. I cried in public or I got angry in public.
Emotions are something we are afraid that we may not have control over. So bhakti is an emotional response to something or someone I identify with. When I identify with someone, my emotional response is to like him or her or it.
So thats an emotional response and that we are very unsure about. Thats what we get afraid of. Everybody says love God.
Every religion says love God. Every teacher says, you should love God. But how should I love God? Nobody has been very clear about this -- love does not come because I try hard.
Trying to love someone is a very difficult thing. Rajan, you should love him. But I dont like him. So we are very unsure about how to engage ourselves in Bhakti Yoga. Therefore, many teachers have defined Bhakti in different ways. There is a very authoritative book called Narada Bhakti Sutra.

These verses present a profound truth about the spiritual path: the abstract, formless approach to the Divine (Avyakta) brings greater hardships (kleso adhikatarah) for those who identify with the body. Krishna is not discouraging the path of formless meditation, but acknowledging a practical reality. The phrase dehavadbhir (for the embodied ones) points to our current condition: we are deeply identified with this physical form, its sensations, its desires, its limitations. To leap from this embodied identification directly to the formless Absolute is like asking someone who has never swum to cross an ocean. The verse about surrendering all actions to the Lord (sarvani karmani mayi sannyasya) offers a more accessible doorway.
The key teaching here is sarvabhutahite ratah, being engaged in the welfare of all beings. True devotion expresses itself not in withdrawal from the world but in compassionate engagement with it. When you serve others seeing them as expressions of the Divine, every interaction becomes worship. This transforms ordinary life into a spiritual practice. Notice how different this is from devotion as mere ritual or sentiment.
Today, practice this: Before each significant interaction, silently acknowledge that the person before you is an expression of the same consciousness that animates you. Whether it is a colleague, a family member, or a stranger, let your actions toward them be offerings to the Divine. At the end of the day, reflect: How did this shift in perspective change the quality of your interactions? Where did you find it easy, and where did resistance arise?
